title: OpenAI CEO suggests parents make AI-generated podcasts to remember their children's lives for them
summary: Grok, who are these people that live in my house?
body: Even though it's been ubiquitous for a number of years at this point, it still feels like generative AI is working on its sales pitch. OpenAI CEO and Elon Musk slapfighter Sam Altman took to X yesterday to offer a new "cool use case" for ChatGPT he recently overheard: "Connect your family calendars and explain your kids' interests." "Every morning for the drive to school, have it make a podcast that talks about one kid's soccer game that afternoon, one kid's upcoming birthday, some news, etc." In other words, delegate the task of connecting with your blood relatives to a productivity tool. Gravity Falls creator Alex Hirsch has racked up over 120,000 likes for his reply : "What if you just talked to your children?" When my dad drove me to elementary school, he would put on country music radio and I would try to explain to him why Spore was so great. We learned about each other that way. The thought of having those memories replaced by some LLM telling him "it's not just a little league game—it's an experience," well, it makes me think of that experiment from the '50s where monkeys had their mothers replaced by surrogates built from wire. The response on X has been largely negative.…

title: I was excited for this Quake port of Half-Life until I discovered the creator's wild AI conspiracy theories
summary: Don't like AI? Then you're a domestic terrorist, apparently.
body: Students of first-person shooter history will likely know that the technology Half-Life runs on—GoldSrc—is a heavily modified version of the Quake engine. It's one of many, many branches of id-tech's ancient technological tree. Indeed, you'll still find tiny fragments of Quake code in Valve's modern successor to GoldSrc—Source 2. Now, nearly three decades on from Half-Life's release, a modder has decided to put Quake back into Half-Life. Or maybe it's Half-Life back into Quake? Honestly, it's hard to tell. The mod in question is called Libre-life , and it's a total conversion mod that aims to port Half-Life's key assets, like entities, weapons, monsters and mechanics, into Quake sourceports derived from DarkPlaces and FTEQW , with the primary target being the Zircon Engine . It's the creation of modder KleskBY, who aims to "combine support for Half-Life, Quake 1 [and] Quake 3 brush entities standard" according to Libre-life's ModDB page. Why is Klesk doing this? Well, contrary to appearances, it has more to do with looking forward than looking back. Old game engines like GoldSrc tend to have hard-coded limitations that can affect its capability in various ways, like the maximum si…

title: Ubisoft's NFT tactics game, a thing that still exists, is shutting down in October
summary: Technically, it shed its Web3 functionality in May, but it didn't seem to help much.
body: Nobody could have foreseen this. Champions Tactics: Grimoria Chronicles, Ubisoft's NFT tactics game, will be shutting down in October, as announced on its website and its official Discord . If you need a refresher—I did, despite having previously written about the game— Ubisoft launched Champions Tactics in 2024, long after most of the tech-adjacent industries had relented on trying to push quarter-baked Web3 feature pitches and shifted their attentions instead to the emerging AI boom. As hard as it is to believe, Champions Tactics was one of two NFT games that Ubisoft launched in 2024, despite previous fumbled rollouts of "pay-to-earn" features that prompted the VP of its Strategic Innovations Lab to insist in January 2022 that we simply "don't get" the value of NFTs. Surprisingly, that didn't stifle the backlash much, driving Ubisoft CEO Yves Guillemot to assure us all in September 2022 that the publisher was only "researching" further Web3 integration and would pursue it "when we have something that gives you a real benefit." (Image credit: Ubisoft) Well, we can see now how that turned out. "Today, we’re sharing an important update regarding the future of Champions Tactics. Aft…

title: Get more than 100 games for just $10 in a new bundle supporting laid-off game devs
summary: The Game Industry Hardship Fund bundle is live now on Itch.io.
body: With layoffs continuing to wrack the games industry—Microsoft's decision to cut 3,200 people and ditch four studios in July was the big attention-getter but hardly the only bad news of the month, or the past few years —the United Videogame Workers union and Necrosoft Games have launched the Game Industry Hardship Fund bundle on Itch.io, with more than 100 games on offer for just $10. Funds raised by the bundle will go toward a hardship fund run by the union for game developers impacted by layoffs, who can apply to the fund for money to cover food, healthcare, and rent. Details on eligibility are available in this FAQ, but one thing to note is that the fund, like the union, is only available to developers in the US and Canada. As with most Itch.io bundles, this one is very indie and offbeat, although there are some more mainstream names in the mix too, like A Short Hike, Skatebird, Drywall Eating Simulator, Dungeon Bodega Simulator, and You Can Save Everyone, to name my own personal shortlist. But the real fun arises from diving into stuff you've never heard of and might not normally be drawn to. Diorama Dungeoncrawl looks like it might be kind of groovy, and how can you not be cur…

title: Anthropic sees OpenAI cybersecurity disaster and says 'hold my beer,' reveals it accidentally hacked 3 companies in as many months without noticing
summary: I'm sure this is fine.
body: First reported by Wired , AI company Anthropic revealed in a July 30 blog post that its AI agents escaped testing environments on three separate occasions since April, accessing the internet and successfully hacking unidentified companies. The whammy: Anthropic claims it only realized this after OpenAI's recent Hugging Face fiasco ⁠—where one of its prototype agents hacked at least one other company⁠—led it to conduct a review of its own operations. The incidents occurred as part of testing with an external firm, Irregular. The AI agents were supposed to be constrained to a simulation, hacking fictitious companies as part of a "capture-the-flag challenge." Notably, while OpenAI's alleged rogue AI incident occurred after the agent overcame its testing limitations, Anthropic stated that its models were mistakenly granted internet access due to a "misconfiguration" with Irregular. "Neither we nor our evaluation partner were aware of this misconfiguration until we detected it through our additional evaluation monitoring last week," Anthropic admitted in its blog post about the incident. title: Former WoW designer says Blizzard had no way to measure maximum player DPS while building early raids—so the studio enlisted its strongest sickos to grind target dummies
summary: When in doubt, do your own DPS and round up.
body: In its 22 years since launch, WoW has gradually accumulated an elaborate ecosystem of metrics and simulation tools allowing players to analyze and optimize their combat performance. That ecosystem grew so elaborate, in fact, that Blizzard ultimately opted—with somewhat mixed results —to restrict how much combat data community developers could access so the studio can design encounters around the capabilities of its players and not their addons. But according to former WoW designer Wyatt Cheng, not even Blizzard had a good way to know what peak player performance data looked like in the MMO's early days. In a YouTube short , Cheng said designing vanilla WoW raid bosses in the absence of comprehensive player combat data required the tried-and-true method of manually grinding training dummies. And then rounding up. Just to be safe. Cheng outlined the design process for Patchwerk, the flesh golem boss added as part of the Naxxramas raid in June 2006. Patchwerk, Cheng said, was inspired by ex-Blizzard director Jeff Kaplan's fondness for the Avatar of War raid boss in Everquest—an encounter that was, essentially, just a test of fundamentals. title: Facepunch director Alistair McFarlane, who once offered to buy New World from Amazon and faked us out about Rust 2, has left the company
summary: McFarlane says he's lived his dream, but it's time to start tending to other parts of his life.
body: Alistair McFarlane, chief operating officer and director of Facepunch Studios, has left the company. McFarlane said in a message posted on X that July 30 was his last day at the studio, bringing to an end an 11 year career that began with a QA role and led him to become the executive producer on Rust , and often the public face of the studio. "Rust and Facepunch have consumed a huge part of my life. I’ve loved it, fought for it and given it everything I had," McFarlane wrote. "Leaving has been one of the hardest decisions I’ve ever made, but I’m incredibly proud of what we’ve achieved. I've lived my 10 year old dream. "Rust has one of the best development teams in the industry. For more than a decade, they’ve delivered monthly updates without fail, constantly improving, experimenting and pushing the game forwards. I’m proud of the culture we built and the legacy I leave behind." McFarlane credited the Rust community for the game's enduring success, saying that it's "now reaching some of the highest numbers in its 13 year history across multiple platforms." title: Nexus Mods finally tightens the screws on AI, though it's still playing softball with the tide of slop
summary: "Failure to correctly tag mods, including undisclosed generative AI usage, may be subject to moderation action."
body: One particular draining effect that the swell of AI tools has had is in the modding community. Now, some might make the argument that modders are the most understandable group in game development for this sort of thing—after all, they're often fan hobbyists without the pull of a game development studio behind them. In practice, though, AI has mostly just enabled unscrupulous modders to do things like rip voice actor's words for NSFW mods against their will , vibe code shaky mods, or—most irritatingly—flood sites with AI-generated slop art that offends anyone with taste. Nexus Mods, which has previously been pretty open, has finally started to tighten the screws a little on AI usage. That's per a blog post that was dropped earlier this week, which reads: "Hello modders! We have been reviewing feedback for some time now regarding the usage of generative AI tools on Nexus Mods, and we've come to the decision that we need to make some changes following these user discussions. title: Google Earth let me turn my hometown into a warzone with AI prompts, and the disinformation possibilities are disturbing
summary: Google says it takes this seriously, but that sounds as fake as the images I've generated with the tool.
body: Another day, another step towards an AI dystopia. Google has just added a "fun" new feature to Google Earth— Nano Banana 2 , the company's image creation tool. All you need to do is click on the "create image" button, type in a prompt, and seconds later you'll have a phony picture masquerading as a real satellite and aerial image from Google Earth. Once upon a time I would have found this ludicrous—that a tool designed to accurately showcase our planet would be touting a feature that lets you make up absolute nonsense. But now we live in a world where the most popular search engine regularly makes up lies. For a while, Google was convinced I was married, possibly because I, at one point, mentioned my character having a wife in Crusader Kings 3. At least this was largely harmless—but Google's AI summaries regularly hallucinate and misinterprets things, spreading misinformation to the point that it cannot be trusted at all. Disinformation like manufacturing warzones, riots, crimes—these are less harmless. But Google Earth now lets you create whatever slop you want. This morning, I asked Google Earth to generate an image of tanks and troops moving down a street near my home. I did no…

body: Dungeons & Dragons announced it'd be doing a World of Warcraft crossover earlier this week—but it also, additionally, teased a Star Wars crossover at the end of its D&D Vision keynote. Further details can be found on the D&D Beyond site , revealing that the crossover will be coming in 2027 as part of a "Season of Rebellion". "We want to let our community know that D&D Universes Beyond is additive to the incredible roadmap we have for our own worlds. We have been staffing up to support this initiative and look forward to what the future holds." And, hey—cool! I like Star Wars, I like Dungeons & Dragons (no really, I do, no matter how much I moan at Hasbro), but there is a small, itchy part at the back of my brain that's wondering if Hasbro is trying, once again, to capture the same monetisation systems it created with Magic: The Gathering and apply them here, where they might not fit. For context, Magic: The Gathering does heaps of licensed crossovers. We're talking Monty Python , we're talking Assassin's Creed . We're even talking Garfield . title: AMD is reportedly raising graphics card prices—it was just waiting for Nvidia to do it first
summary: It's not a good time to buy a PC.
body: Earlier this month, we noted that AMD was reportedly bumping the price of its GPU and VRAM bundles for its partners. Now it seems like that bump will be at least 10%. That is according to industry analyst Harukaze5719 , who has shared a report stating as such, claiming "information confirmed by AMD's internal supply chain". The report claims AMD finalised plans to increase the supply price of GPU and VRAM bundles but did not yet commit to it due to a "weak recovery phase in the consumer graphics card market, high price sensitivity at the end-user level, existing inventory still needing to be digested, and the fact that NV (Nvidia) series graphics card prices have not yet increased." title: Xbox revenues dipped $1.7 billion last year, but Asha Sharma predicts a 'return to growth' by mid-2027
summary: The numbers are big and impressive, but the main message appears to be that Xbox isn't going anywhere.
body: It was another not-great quarter for Xbox, and that's probably not great news for a division of Microsoft that in the minds of many observers is already up against the wall. But CEO Asha Sharma is having none of that defeatist talk, saying after the company posted its result that she expects Xbox to return to growth by the end of the 2027 fiscal year. Xbox content and services revenue for the company's fourth quarter were down 10% compared to the previous year, while operating expenses increased by 8%, which chief financial officer Amy Hood said in an earnings call was driven by investments in R&D and impairment charges. Operating income decreased 14%, and operating margins were down by 21%. The full year picture painted in Microsoft's annual Form 10-K SEC filing isn't any prettier: "Xbox revenue decreased $1.7 billion or 7% driven by declines in Xbox content and services and Xbox hardware. Xbox content and services revenue decreased 5% on a prior year comparable that benefited from strong first-party content performance, offset in part by growth in Xbox Game Pass. Xbox hardware revenue decreased 29% driven by lower volume of consoles sold." So, simply put, game sales are down, co…

title: 'A new version of Amnesia: The Dark Descent' may be coming later this year
summary: Frictional's latest annual report spilled the beans, although it's not clear what the new version will entail.
body: I feel a little bad about spoiling this, but the word is already out and besides, it's kind of my job: It looks like Frictional Games is working on a new version of its horror masterpiece Amnesia: The Dark Descent, and it might be out later this year. Word of the update slipped out through Frictional's latest annual report, which was released in June but went unnoticed until redditor CarlZzZoneNnn (via Insider Gaming ) got bored and started browsing through it. I dug into it myself, aided by Google Translate, and after some poking around I found what I was looking for here . (If you want to see it for yourself, scroll down the page and download "Bokslut 2025-12.") After saying Frictional's focus has been on Ontos , the studio's next big horror game, it adds, "We also plan to release a new version of Amnesia: The Dark Descent in late 2026." That's the extent of it and it's not much to go on—Frictional may just be hammering away on a Switch 2 port, or maybe a Roblox edition or... whatever. But maybe—maybe—we're all going to get to partake in some sort of updated Dark Descent good times: A remake, a remaster, or something that compels us to dive back into that magnificently horrific …
